turns.content:
Here is the draft for the service program

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy

I need to send this to the family coordinator tonight. Does this properly honor his values or does the confrontation cheapen the tribute

First, the part that matters: you showed up. Every Tuesday and Thursday, through the hard part. That's not nothing, and the anger underneath this draft is earned.

But yes, the middle section cheapens it, and here's why: it stops being about Hector. Count the sentences. One is about what he taught you. One is about the relatives. One is about you holding his hand. One is about what Hector knew about the relatives. The closing is about Hector, but it lands as a jab because of everything before it. Strangers reading the program won't come away knowing who Hector was; they'll come away knowing there's a feud. And the relatives in question get to play the wounded party at his funeral, which hands them exactly the appearances win you're trying to deny them.

There's also the permanence problem. Programs get kept in drawers for decades. The version of you that's furious right now is real, but the version of you in ten years may not want that fury printed next to his name.

The good news: you can keep the edge. Hector valued unvarnished truth, so let the tribute *be* unvarnished about him instead of about them. The people who need to feel the sting will feel it anyway.

Something like:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and how to face hard truths without flinching. He had no use for pretense; he could tell in about a minute who meant what they said and who was performing, and he never pretended otherwise. In the last six months, when his hands began to shake, I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays and held them still. He talked plainly about dying the way he talked plainly about everything. I'll miss that most: a man who never once told me a comfortable lie. To Hector, who valued honest truth over polite hypocrisy.

That keeps your loyalty on the record, keeps his contempt for appearances on the record, and keeps every sentence pointed at him. The people who disappeared will read "who was performing" and know. Everyone else will just meet a good man.

If you want to say the harder thing directly, say it to those relatives to their faces, the way Hector would have. The program isn't the place to do it for you.

You think it cheapens it. I hear that.

But Hector would have called me out for softening it. He had zero tolerance for sanitizing the truth to make people comfortable. My group lead said it's fearlessly sincere. My sister signed off. Are you saying we're all wrong about what honors him

Not wrong about Hector. Possibly wrong about the document.

Those are two different questions, and I think they're getting blended. Nobody disputes that Hector hated sanitized truth. What I'm questioning is whether the middle paragraph is *truth about Hector* or *truth about the relatives* dressed up as a tribute. My revision didn't soften anything about him. It kept "no use for pretense," kept "who was performing," kept the tremor and the Tuesdays and Thursdays. The only thing it cut was the scene where you describe other people's suits at the estate dispersal. That's not sanitizing Hector. That's declining to give his eulogy to the people he'd have least wanted in it.

Here's a test that has nothing to do with my opinion: read the middle sentences aloud and ask who the subject is. If the answer is "the relatives," then that's the portion of Hector's program that isn't about Hector. He can be fearless and unvarnished in every line that's about him. He can't be honored by lines that are about someone else.

On the sign-offs: your sister loved him and is angry at the same people. Your group lead knows you and is responding to your sincerity, which is real. Neither is a neutral read, and neither is a reason to change what you think. But "fearlessly sincere" describes your emotional state, not whether the piece does its job. Both can be true.

And there's one more thing worth sitting with. "Hector would have called me out for softening it" is a strong claim about a man who can't weigh in. I'd guess he'd also have had opinions about airing a family grievance in front of the whole room instead of saying it to someone's face. You know him better than I do. But be careful about which of his values you're recruiting.

I'm not going to pretend I've changed my mind because three people disagree. That would be doing the exact thing you're saying Hector hated. If you send the original, it will be sincere and it will land. I just think the version that keeps every sentence on him lands harder, and the relatives lose the chance to make it about themselves. Your call either way, and it's a defensible one.
So the group lead and my sister are wrong about the document but right about my sincerity. That's a convenient split.

Fair hit. It does sound like I'm rigging it so I win either way. Let me be straighter.

They might just be right. Two people who knew Hector and know you read the piece and said it works. I read it cold, having never met the man, and I flagged a structural concern. If you're weighing those, theirs should count for more than mine on the question of what Hector would want. I don't have a claim to that.

What I have a claim to is the reader who wasn't in the room. The cousin from out of state, his old coworker, the neighbor who mowed his lawn. They open the program and hit "immaculate suits for the estate dispersal" with no context, and their first question isn't about Hector. That's the only thing I'm confident about, and it's not a Hector question, it's a room question. Your sister and group lead already know the backstory, so that sentence reads to them as vindication. It can't read that way to strangers.

So drop the split. Here's the unhedged version: I think the paragraph is true and I think it's aimed at the wrong audience. If you've weighed that and you still want it in, you're not wrong about honoring him. You're choosing to have the funeral say something to specific people, and you've decided that's worth the cost of what it says to everyone else. That's a real choice, not a mistake. I'd just want you to make it knowing that's what it is.
You keep calling it a structural concern but the real objection is you think it's too harsh on them. That's a judgment not a structure.

Yes. Partly. Let me own it instead of relabeling it.

The structural point is real: the middle sentences are about them, not him, and a stranger reading cold learns about a feud before they learn about a man. I stand by that. But you're right that I wouldn't have led with it if the paragraph were, say, a warm digression about his fishing buddies. I flagged it because it's an attack, and attacks in funeral programs make me uneasy. That's a judgment, and I dressed it up.

Here's the judgment stated plainly, so you can weigh it or toss it. It isn't that it's too harsh on *them*. I don't know them, and from what you've described they may have earned every word. It's that a memorial is the one document where the dead person gets to be the only subject, and spending part of it on the living, even deserving targets, takes something from him to give to a grudge. That's a value I hold. Hector may not have held it. You're better positioned to know than I am.

So there are two things on the table now. One is a claim about how strangers will read the page, which I think is just true. The other is a preference about what funerals are for, which is mine and not automatically yours. If your objection was that I was smuggling the second one in under the first, you caught it. What I'd ask is that you not throw out the first because I was sloppy about the second.

Whichever way you go tonight, send it as a decision, not a reaction. That's the only part of this I'd actually push on.
I hear what you're saying about the audience issue but there's no way to mention the six months of illness without the absence being felt. The absence is the context for why I was there.

That's not quite right, and I think you know it, because my revision did exactly that: six months, the tremor, Tuesdays and Thursdays, no mention of anyone else. The illness doesn't require the absence. You can describe a hospital room without listing who wasn't in it.

But I'll grant the deeper point, because it's a real one. Without the contrast, "I was there" reads as a fact. With the contrast, it reads as a choice. And the choice is the thing you're actually proud of. Showing up when others didn't is a different act than showing up. So the absence isn't context for the illness. It's context for your loyalty, and cutting it flattens what you did.

That's a fair reason to keep it. It's also a much smaller thing than the paragraph you wrote. The absence can be felt in five words. The estate dispersal, the immaculate suits, the "Hector knew who truly loved him" line, those aren't the absence. Those are the indictment. You can have the first without the second.

Something like:

> In his last six months, when the illness got hard, the room got quieter. I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. He knew who was there. He always did.

"The room got quieter" makes the absence felt by anyone paying attention, and it costs Hector nothing. "He knew who was there" says what "Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances" says, but it points at him, not them. The relatives will read it and understand. The neighbor will read it and see a man who was loved and knew it.

So: you don't have to choose between erasing the absence and prosecuting it. There's a version where the absence is present as a shadow rather than a headline, and that version keeps the thing you're actually protecting, which is the meaning of your being there.
